summary: Summarizes the answers sites gave to the host questionnaire introduced in RFC 106. The chart shows how different hosts handle terminals, especially line-at-a-time versus character-at-a-time input and control characters. It was meant as background for people implementing Telnet. Dated April 1, 1971, but it is not a joke.

eli5.summary: Lots of families answered a survey about their TVs. This is the chart of the answers, so toy makers can see how different the TVs are.

subtitle: A 1971 chart of how ARPANET sites handled terminals, gathered to help the people designing TELNET.

tldr.problem: The committee designing TELNET needed to know how different host computers handled user terminals, especially control characters.
tldr.mechanism: The author summarized the answers to a host questionnaire (referenced as RFC 106) in a chart titled ARPA Network User Terminal Support.
tldr.outcome: The chart shows key differences between line-at-a-time and character-at-a-time terminal handling, as background for TELNET implementers. The chart itself is only in the PDF version.

today: RFC 112 is an early ARPANET note, and its status is listed as Unknown. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a historical record of terminal differences among early hosts.

sections.title: The Questionnaire Summary
sections.content:
RFC 112 is a one-page cover note by T. O'Sullivan of Raytheon Data Systems, dated April 1, 1971. It is not a joke despite the date. It attaches a summary of the responses to questionnaires referenced as RFC 106 (NIC Note 5776).

The questions about terminal support were of interest to members of the User/Service Site Protocol Committee while it considered TELNET.
sections.eli5: Someone asked every site the same questions and wrote the answers on one big chart.

sections.title: Line-at-a-Time or Character-at-a-Time
sections.content:
The summary points out some of the key differences between line-at-a-time and character-at-a-time (or both) in handling terminal support. The differences matter most for control characters.

The RFC says the information may prove useful as background for TELNET implementers. The chart is not reproduced in the plain-text version, which points readers to the PDF.
sections.eli5: Some computers wait until you finish a whole line before looking at it. Others look at every letter as you type. The chart shows which sites do which.

sections.title: Corrections Welcome
sections.content: The author asks that anyone who finds an error of interpretation in a site's answer let him know at the address given, so that he can update the chart. The address is Raytheon Data Systems in Norwood, Massachusetts.
sections.eli5: If the chart got your answer wrong, you can write to the author and he will fix it.

references.text: User/Server Site Protocol: Network Host Questionnaire, RFC 106, NIC Note 5776.
